# Task B2.4 — Root-Cause Analysis: The 8.4% Book-vs-Physical Stock Variance

**Client:** Savanna Retail Group (SRG) — Kampala, Uganda
**Competency:** C4 (Data Quality) — hands-on
**Evidence base:** `module2_data_quality/output/stock_variance_fishbone.svg` (generated by `make_fishbone.py`), `module2_data_quality/output/before_after_metrics.md`, `validation_rules.md` (VR-001…VR-012), `dq_monitoring_spec.md` (DQC-01…DQC-10), `module3_etl/etl_diagnosis.md` (RC-1…RC-6), `docs/C2_threat_model_risk_register.md` (R6)

---

## 1. The problem, stated as a measurable defect

Book stock (what Odoo/the POS believes) minus physical stock (what a count finds) across all stores averages **8.4% variance** — reported in the scenario as *"nobody knows why"*. Two properties drive the analysis:

1. The variance is **systemic** — it appears at every store, not one, which rules out a single-site explanation (theft at one branch, one bad manager).
2. It is **unattributed** — no store keeps an adjustment log, so the gap cannot currently be split between *process loss*, *measurement error*, and *capture error*. That split is exactly what this analysis sets up.

## 2. Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram

Six cause categories are examined — People, Method, Measurement, Systems, Data, Environment — and every leaf cause is classified by fix type:

![Figure B2.1 — Ishikawa (fishbone) analysis of the 8.4% stock variance. Red = systemic cause (fix the process); blue = point-of-entry cause (validate at capture). Source: `module2_data_quality/output/stock_variance_fishbone.svg`, generated by `make_fishbone.py`.](../portfolio/figures/B2_stock_variance_fishbone.png)

*The diagram distinguishes the two classes the brief demands: **systemic causes** (red — design defects that will keep producing variance no matter how careful individuals are) versus **point-of-entry causes** (blue — defects introduced at the moment of capture and stoppable by validation).*

## 3. Cause classification

| # | Cause (from diagram) | Class | Why it produces variance | Fix that stops it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cashiers edit stock counts by hand at the till | **Point-of-entry** | A count "corrected" to match expectation silently changes book stock | POS stock-adjust permission removed from cashier role; adjustment approval workflow (RBAC, `data_masking.sql` principle extended to Odoo) |
| 2 | No adjustment approval authority | **Systemic** | Anyone may post a correction, so errors and cover-ups are indistinguishable | Adjustment workflow: staff propose → store manager approves → log retained |
| 3 | Inter-store transfers not posted by store teams | **Point-of-entry** | Goods physically move; neither side's book stock follows → both stores diverge in opposite directions | Transfer document with mandatory scan-out/scan-in; DQC variance check per transfer |
| 4 | No cycle-count calendar | **Systemic** | Detection happens only at the annual/periodic count — too late to attribute cause | ABC cycle counts (A monthly, B quarterly, C annually); variance dashboard per store from month 4 (D1 quick win) |
| 5 | Returns processed offline, keyed later | **Systemic** | The 500 return lines (−UGX 10,224,221) re-enter days late; book stock disagrees with shelf in the interim | Returns posted at point of return via the same ETL contract; quarantine if late (RC-1/RC-4 fix) |
| 6 | Shrink never audited (theft unlogged) | **Systemic** | Shrinkage has no book entry at all — it accumulates as variance by definition | Shrink allowance surfaced as drift in the real-time consumer (`B4_realtime_architecture.md`) + monthly shrink report to Store Operations Manager |
| 7 | Five competing product identifiers | **Systemic** | The same SKU counts under different IDs at different stores — books compare non-comparable quantities | Crosswalk to golden SKU (B3 MDM); VR-001…VR-007 at capture; DQC-06 SKU uniqueness |
| 8 | UOM kg / KGS / Kilograms typed freely (15.33% non-conformance pre-cleanse) | **Point-of-entry** | A 2 kg bag entered as "2" while another store enters "2,000 g" — unit errors scale into valuation errors | UOM standardisation list in entry forms (VR-004); conformance DQC-04 (100% after cleanse) |
| 9 | Hand-written count sheets | **Point-of-entry** | Transcription errors enter book stock a second time | Tablet count forms with validation; count variance sign-off |
| 10 | 23 MySQL silos, no unified stock ledger | **Systemic** | No single quantity exists to compare against — "book stock" is 23 private opinions | Warehouse `fact_sales` + Odoo feed (M8) as the single stock ledger |
| 11 | Offline POS sales sync when connectivity returns | **Systemic** | Hours of sales invisible to book stock → phantom stock → stock-outs and overstock both explained | Store-and-forward with sequence numbers; lag surfaced, not hidden (PENDING_RECON pattern applied to stock) |
| 12 | No audit trail on quantity changes | **Systemic** | Nobody can split the 8.4% into causes *today* — the measurement itself is missing | Quantity-change audit table (who/when/old/new/reason) — prerequisite for attribution |
| 13 | Duplicate SKUs across POS / e-commerce / supplier files | **Systemic** | Physical goods counted once, books recorded under 2+ identities | Dedupe + golden product (B2 cleanse: composite validity 3.25% → 100%) |
| 14 | Category typos break like-for-like counts | **Point-of-entry** | Category-level roll-ups double-count one class and miss another | Standardised category list (VR-005); 22% → 100% conformance |
| 15 | Supplier Excel variants of the same product | **Systemic** | Goods-in books a description the stores do not use | Supplier file contract → golden SKU mapping at ingestion |
| 16 | Connectivity loss hours daily (store reality) | **Systemic** | Everything queued syncs in a burst; partial states are visible to customers but not to books | Sequence-numbered replay + lag KPI (see #11) |
| 17 | Power outages — UPS-only tills | **Systemic** | A till that dies mid-transaction loses the stock movement entirely | Transaction journal persisted locally, replayed on restart (ETL idempotency pattern RC-4) |
| 18 | Shop-floor piloting at busy stores | **Point-of-entry** | Stock lifted without a sale recorded — honest shoppers, broken books | CCTV-linked cycle counts at high-shrink stores; adjustment approval (#2) |

**Class split: 11 systemic, 7 point-of-entry.** That ratio is the finding: cleansing at entry (blue) would recover at most ~39% of the identified causes; the remaining 61% are produced by *process design* and will regenerate the variance no matter how carefully staff type. This is why a one-off stock-take cannot fix 8.4%.

## 4. Five-Whys (two branches, showing where they converge)

**Branch A — a counted unit is simply missing (shrink/wastage path):**

1. *Why is stock missing?* It left the store without a book entry.
2. *Why without a book entry?* No adjustment/shrink transaction type is used at store level.
3. *Why not?* No one is accountable — adjustments have no approval authority.
4. *Why no authority?* The operating model never assigned stock ownership below HQ.
5. *Why?* Inventory was managed as a finance number, not an operational one → **root: no named stock owner in the governance model (fixed by A2 ownership roles + D1 KPI ownership).**

**Branch B — a counted unit is present but mis-booked (measurement path):**

1. *Why does book ≠ shelf?* The booked quantity is under a different ID/UOM than the counted one.
2. *Why?* Five product IDs and free-text UOM were never reconciled.
3. *Why not?* Each system validated its own entries only — no enterprise keys.
4. *Why?* No master data and no entry validation existed (23% duplicate customers are the same disease in customer space).
5. *Why?* Data was a by-product, not a managed asset → **root: no MDM, no validation at capture (fixed by B3 golden record + VR-001…VR-012).**

Both branches converge on the same conclusion as Task A1: the variance is a **governance** symptom, not a counting problem.

## 5. Systemic vs point-of-entry: what gets done first

| | Point-of-entry causes (7) | Systemic causes (11) |
|---|---|---|
| **Stop-the-bleeding (M1–M6)** | Entry validation lists (UOM, category, SKU), removal of cashier stock-edit rights, mandatory transfer posting | Adjustment approval workflow, quantity-change audit table, quarantine + replay for offline syncs |
| **Structural fix (M4–M12)** | Tablet count forms | Single stock ledger (Odoo feed M8), golden SKU crosswalk, sequence-numbered store-and-forward |
| **Detection** | VR checks at capture block the defect | DQC-06/DQC-07 daily variance thresholds alert the on-call rotation |
| **Target** | Validity/conformance 100% at entry | Book-vs-physical variance ≤2.0% by M12 (D1 KPI), ≤1.5% at 18 months |

## 6. Process changes (not data fixes) — the brief's explicit demand

1. **Ownership, not correction.** Stock ownership moves into the A2 operating structure: Merchandising Owner + Store Operations Manager hold the variance KPI; adjustments require an approver (name in POL-001 enforcement column).
2. **Count as routine.** ABC cycle counts replace the annual scramble; counts are posted the same day (no sheet transcription).
3. **Every movement is a transaction.** Transfers, returns, shrink, adjustments all become typed events consumed by the repaired ETL — the same idempotent, quarantined contract that fixed RC-1…RC-6 for sales.
4. **Variance becomes visible per store.** The real-time stock consumer surfaces *drift* (book vs projected) within 30–60 s of a sync, so a store manager sees divergence before the count does.
5. **Attribution before punishment.** The audit table exists first so shrink can be *measured*; until 8.4% is decomposed into the five buckets, no store is judged on the number — this is also the change-management safeguard against under-reporting.

## 7. Think-deeper answer

The defect classes look like typing problems, but the causal chain runs through process and incentive design. The blue (point-of-entry) causes stop at the form: a validation list, a blocked field, a permission removed. The red (systemic) causes regenerate themselves — an unowned process produces variance *by design*, then a "clean-up exercise" repairs the number, and six months later the same stores report the same gap, because nothing about the creation, approval, or audit of stock movements changed. That is the identical pattern A1 documents for customers (23% duplicates returning after every cleanse): **cleansing without enforcement is a recurring cost, not an improvement.** The process changes that end it are unglamorous — named owners, an approval step, an audit table, a count calendar — and they are precisely the cheap, technical controls the four-person IT team can run, because they live in the flow of work rather than in a policy binder.
